newsitem.title: USA: Witnesses describe killings in Tiananmen Square.
newsitem.headline: Witnesses describe killings in Tiananmen Square.

text.p: Witnesses at a U.S. House hearing on Wednesday said they saw scores of people killed by Chinese troops during the 1989 pro-democracy demonstrations at Beijing's Tiananmen Square.

The House Human Rights Subcommittee hearing was called to challenge a statement last week by Chinese Defence Minister Chi Haotian during his U.S. visit that no one was killed at Tiananmen Square when Chinese troops crushed the protests.
Jian-il Yang said he saw Chinese soliders firing automatic weapons at the demonstrators early on morning of June 4, 1989.
"Each time they fired weapons, three or four people were hit, and each time the crowd went down on the ground. I saw 13 people killed," Yang, a research associate at Harvard, said.
"One officer drew his gun and shot dead a young man who was standing about nine feet from me," Yang added.
Xuecan Wu, a former editor at the People's Daily, said he saw people crushed by armoured personnel carriers as they tried to flee on the evening of June 3 and the morning of June 4.
"Between 1:30 am and 4 am, I saw at least 30 three-wheel carts and hand carts carrying dead and wounded people. Some of the dead had been shot in the head," Wu said.

Louisa Coan of Amnesty International USA said China has refused to allow outside investigators to determine if people were killed in Tiananmen Square itself. "What we do know is that at least 1,000 deaths on the streets surrounding the square, as well as in numerous other areas of Beijing and in other cities in China, are well documented by witnesses and extensive video footage," she said.
Subcommittee Chairman Chris Smith, who scheduled the hearing, said Chi had been invited to offer evidence to support his statement but had not responded.

"By telling us in what he called a 'responsible and serious manner' that 'not a single person lost his life in Tiananmen Square' ... he told us all we needed to know -- and that is that Chi cannot be trusted," Smith said.
The New Jersey Republican is a frequent critic of U.S. policy on China and wants trade to be linked to human rights.
"Chi's visit to the U.S. was a blantant display of how we continue to downplay the importance of human rights," New Jersey Democrat Donald Payne added.
Chi, winding up his U.S. visit in Hawaii, had a 30-minute telephone call on Tuesday with U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, who was in Belgium for a NATO meeting.

Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon said both men stressed the importance of improving bilateral relations, despite disputes over arms proliferation, human rights, trade and Taiwan, which Beijing considers a renegade province of China.
